sections.title: Kana, kanji and pronunciation
sections.summary: Japanese is written with three scripts (hiragana, katakana and kanji) and is pronounced in even, syllable-like beats called morae. This chapter covers the sound system, the voicing marks, double consonants, long vowels and the three particles that are not pronounced as they are written.

rules.title: Three scripts in one sentence
rules.body: Japanese mixes three scripts. Hiragana (ひらがな) is a syllabary used for grammatical endings, particles and native words; katakana (カタカナ) is a parallel syllabary used for foreign loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and emphasis; kanji (漢字) are characters of Chinese origin used for the roots of nouns, verbs and adjectives. A typical sentence combines all three: 私はコーヒーを飲みます.

examples.target: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。

rules.title: Five vowels and the kana grid
rules.body: Japanese has five vowels, a i u e o, pronounced short and pure: あ い う え お. Most other kana are one consonant plus one vowel (か き く け こ = ka ki ku ke ko, and so on down the rows k, s, t, n, h, m, y, r, w). Each kana takes one beat of time; the nasal ん is a beat of its own. There is no stress accent like English, so keep every beat even.

rules.title: Irregular readings in the grid
rules.body: A few kana do not follow the pattern. し is shi (not si), ち is chi, つ is tsu, ふ is fu (a soft sound between f and h), and を as a word particle is pronounced o. The r sound (ら り る れ ろ) is a light tap between English r, l and d. In Hepburn romanization these spellings are standard: shi, chi, tsu, fu.

rules.title: Dakuten and handakuten: voicing marks
rules.body: Two small strokes (dakuten ゛) placed at the top right of a kana make the consonant voiced: か ka becomes が ga, さ sa becomes ざ za, た ta becomes だ da, は ha becomes ば ba. A small circle (handakuten ゜) is used only on the h row and turns it into p: は becomes ぱ pa. The same marks work on katakana: カ → ガ, ハ → パ.

rules.title: Small つ: the double consonant
rules.body: A small っ (ッ in katakana) is not pronounced on its own; it doubles the following consonant and takes one full beat of silence or holding. きって kitte (stamp) sounds different from きて kite (come). In romanization the consonant is written twice: がっこう gakkō, ざっし zasshi, いっぱい ippai.

rules.title: Long vowels
rules.body: A long vowel lasts two beats and changes meaning: おばさん obasan is aunt, おばあさん obāsan is grandmother. In hiragana a long vowel is written by adding a vowel kana: ああ, いい, うう, and for long o usually おう (とうきょう Tōkyō), sometimes おお (おおきい ōkii); long e is usually えい (えいが eiga). In katakana a long vowel is written with a bar: コーヒー kōhī. Hepburn marks long a, o and u with a macron (ā ō ū) and writes long i as ii.

rules.title: Combined sounds with small や・ゆ・よ
rules.body: A kana from the i column followed by a small ゃ ゅ ょ forms a single beat: きゃ kya, きゅ kyu, きょ kyo, しゃ sha, しゅ shu, しょ sho, ちゃ cha, にゃ nya, ひょ hyo, りょ ryo. The small kana is written smaller and must not be read as a separate syllable: びょういん byōin (hospital) has a small ょ, びよういん biyōin (beauty salon) has a full-size よ.

rules.title: Particles は, へ and を have special readings
rules.body: Three kana are read differently when they work as grammatical particles. The topic particle は is pronounced wa (not ha), the direction particle へ is pronounced e (not he), and the object particle を is pronounced o. Inside ordinary words these kana keep their normal sounds: はな hana (flower), へや heya (room). Hepburn writes the particles as wa, e, o.

rules.title: Kanji readings: on and kun
rules.body: Most kanji have at least two readings: a Chinese-derived on reading, used mostly in compounds (学 gaku in 学生 gakusei), and a native kun reading, used when the character stands alone or with hiragana endings (学ぶ manabu, to learn). Hiragana written over kanji to show the reading is called furigana. Beginners learn kanji word by word rather than reading by reading.

exercises.q: Which script is used for loanwords such as コーヒー (coffee)?
exercises.explain: Katakana is the script for foreign loanwords, foreign names and emphasis.

exercises.q: Japanese has five basic vowels: a, i, u, e, o.
exercises.explain: The vowel row あ い う え お gives the five short vowels of Japanese.

exercises.q: Adding dakuten (゛) to か gives ___ (ga).
exercises.explain: Dakuten voices the consonant, so k becomes g.

exercises.q: How is the topic particle は pronounced?
exercises.explain: As a particle は is read wa; inside words it is still ha.

exercises.answer: これ は ペン です

exercises.q: The small っ in きって doubles the following consonant: kitte.
exercises.explain: Small っ holds the next consonant for a full beat, written as a double letter in romanization.

exercises.q: How is 東京 written in Hepburn romanization with macrons?
exercises.explain: Both o sounds are long (とうきょう), and Hepburn marks long o with a macron.

exercises.q: Write 'coffee' in katakana with the long-vowel bar: ___
exercises.explain: Katakana marks long vowels with the bar ー, so both syllables are lengthened.

exercises.q: Which Hepburn spelling is used for the kana ふ?
exercises.explain: ふ is the u kana of the h row and is written fu; its sound is between f and h.

exercises.q: Katakana is used mainly for native Japanese words.
exercises.explain: Native words use hiragana and kanji; katakana is for loanwords, foreign names and emphasis.

exercises.q: Write 'sushi' in hiragana: ___
exercises.explain: す is su and し is shi, so sushi is すし.

exercises.answer: 私 は 日本 へ 行きます

exercises.q: How is the object particle を pronounced?
exercises.explain: The particle を is pronounced o in modern Japanese; Hepburn writes it o.

exercises.q: In がっこう (school) the small っ means the k is held: gakkō.
exercises.explain: Small っ doubles the following consonant and the おう is a long o.

exercises.q: In Hepburn the direction particle へ is written ___ (one letter).
exercises.explain: As a particle へ loses its h sound and is pronounced e.

exercises.q: Which spelling means 'grandmother' (obāsan), with a long vowel?
exercises.explain: The extra あ makes a two-beat long vowel; おばさん with a short a means aunt.

exercises.answer: ここ は 学校 です

exercises.q: Kanji are characters of Chinese origin used for the roots of nouns, verbs and adjectives.
exercises.explain: Kanji carry the meaning of content words while hiragana supplies endings and particles.

exercises.q: In Hepburn romanization し is written:
exercises.explain: Hepburn spells the irregular s-row kana as shi to reflect its sound.

exercises.q: Romanize おとうさん (father) in Hepburn with a macron: ___
exercises.explain: おう is a long o, written ō in Hepburn.

exercises.q: What does the handakuten ゜ turn は into?
exercises.explain: The small circle is used only on the h row and makes it p.

exercises.q: The kana ん takes a full beat of its own and can end a word.
exercises.explain: ん is the only kana without a vowel; にほん Nihon has three beats, ending in ん.

exercises.answer: 日本語 は おもしろい です

exercises.q: Romanize きって (postage stamp) in Hepburn: ___
exercises.explain: The small っ doubles the t of て.

sections.title: The core particles は, が, を, の
sections.summary: Japanese marks the job of each noun with a particle placed after it. This chapter covers the four most important ones: は for the topic, が for the subject, を for the object and の for possession and linking nouns.

rules.title: は marks the topic
rules.body: The particle は (pronounced wa) follows the thing the sentence is about: 私は学生です literally means 'as for me, (I) am a student'. The topic is usually something already known to both speakers, and the rest of the sentence is a comment on it. A topic can be the person doing the action, a time, a place or even an object.

examples.en: Today is hot. (As for today, it is hot.)

examples.target: 田中さんは日本人です。

rules.title: が marks the subject and new information
rules.body: The particle が follows the grammatical subject, especially when it is new information or the answer to a question. Question words that are the subject (誰 who, 何 what, どれ which) always take が, never は, and the answer to such a question also uses が: 誰が来ますか — 田中さんが来ます. Natural phenomena being reported as new (雨が降っています) also take が.

rules.title: は versus が
rules.body: は introduces what the sentence is about; が identifies who or what does something. In 象は鼻が長いです (as for elephants, the nose is long) the elephant is the topic and the nose is the subject of 'long'. Use は when the focus is on the comment and が when the focus is on the subject itself: 私は田中です answers 'who are you?', 私が田中です answers 'which one is Tanaka?'.

examples.roman: Zō wa hana ga nagai desu.
examples.en: Elephants have long trunks. (As for elephants, the nose is long.)
I am Tanaka. (I am the one who is Tanaka.)

rules.title: を marks the direct object
rules.body: The particle を (pronounced o) follows the thing that receives the action of a verb: 水を飲みます (drink water), 本を読みます (read a book), 日本語を勉強します (study Japanese). It is used only with transitive verbs, and the object normally comes right before the verb.

rules.title: を with movement through or out of a place
rules.body: With verbs of motion, を marks the place that is passed through or left: 公園を歩きます (walk through the park), 道を渡ります (cross the street), 家を出ます (leave the house), 電車を降ります (get off the train). The place is treated as the thing the movement covers.

rules.title: の: possession and linking nouns
rules.body: の joins two nouns, with the first describing the second: 私の本 (my book), 田中さんの車 (Mr Tanaka's car). It also expresses origin, type and belonging, where English might use 'of' or an adjective: 日本語の先生 (a teacher of Japanese), 東京の大学 (a university in Tokyo), 友達の田中さん (my friend Tanaka). Several の can be chained: 私の友達の車.

rules.title: の as a pronoun: 'the one'
rules.body: When the noun is obvious, の alone can stand for it, like English 'one' or 'mine': 私のです (it is mine), 赤いのをください (give me the red one), 大きいのが好きです (I like the big one). This の follows a possessor or an adjective and takes a particle after it just like a noun.

examples.en: Please give me the red one.

rules.title: が with certain predicates
rules.body: Some predicates take が where English would expect an object. 好き (like), 嫌い (dislike), わかる (understand), できる (can do), ほしい (want), 上手 (good at) and the existence verbs ある/いる all mark the thing in question with が: 寿司が好きです, 日本語がわかります. If that thing is also the topic, は replaces が: 日本語はわかります.

rules.title: は for contrast and in negative sentences
rules.body: は can replace を or が (and follow other particles) to single out an item for contrast, and this is very common in negative sentences: 肉は食べません (meat, I don't eat), 東京には行きません (to Tokyo I'm not going). Two は in one sentence often signal a contrast: 魚は食べますが、肉は食べません.

examples.target: 魚は食べますが、肉は食べません。
examples.roman: Sakana wa tabemasu ga, niku wa tabemasen.
examples.en: I eat fish, but I don't eat meat.

exercises.q: Introducing yourself: 私___学生です。
exercises.explain: は marks the topic, 'as for me, I am a student'.

exercises.q: 水___飲みます。(object particle)
exercises.explain: を marks the direct object of 飲みます.

exercises.q: The topic particle は is pronounced wa.
exercises.explain: As a particle は keeps its old reading wa; inside words it is ha.

exercises.answer: 私 は 本 を 読みます

exercises.q: これは私___本です。(This is my book.)
exercises.explain: の links the possessor to the thing possessed.

exercises.q: 誰___来ましたか。(Who came? question word as subject)
exercises.explain: A question word that is the subject always takes が.

exercises.q: Question words such as 誰 and 何 take は when they are the subject.
exercises.explain: They take が, because a question word can never be a known topic.

exercises.q: 'a teacher of Japanese': 日本語___先生
exercises.explain: の joins two nouns, the first describing the second.

exercises.answer: 田中さん は 日本語 の 先生 です
exercises.en: Mr Tanaka is a teacher of Japanese.

exercises.q: 公園___歩きます。(walk through the park)
exercises.explain: を marks the place that a movement passes through.

exercises.q: Which sentence means 'Elephants have long trunks' (as for elephants, the nose is long)?
exercises.explain: The elephant is the topic (は) and the nose is the subject (が) of 'long'.

exercises.q: の can join two nouns so that the first describes the second: 東京の大学 'a university in Tokyo'.
exercises.explain: の covers possession, origin and type, not just ownership.

exercises.q: Reporting the weather: 雨___降っています。(It is raining.)
exercises.explain: New information such as a natural event is introduced with が.

exercises.q: 肉___食べません。(meat, I don't eat; contrast)
exercises.explain: は replaces を to single out the object, especially in negative sentences.

exercises.answer: 猫 が います

exercises.q: Which particle goes with 好き? 寿司___好きです。
exercises.explain: 好き is an adjective-like predicate whose object takes が.

exercises.q: 赤いの can mean 'the red one'.
exercises.explain: の stands in for an obvious noun after an adjective or possessor.

exercises.q: 日本語___わかります。(I understand Japanese)
exercises.explain: わかる marks what is understood with が, not を.

exercises.q: Asking which person is the teacher: 誰___先生ですか。
exercises.explain: 誰 as the subject must take が.

exercises.answer: これ は 誰 の かばん です か

exercises.q: を marks the direct object and is pronounced o.
exercises.explain: The particle を has lost its w sound in modern Japanese.

exercises.q: 家___出ます。(leave the house)
exercises.explain: The place you leave is marked with を after a verb of motion.

exercises.q: 私は寿司___食べます。でも、ラーメン___食べません。Which pair of particles fits?
exercises.explain: The first object takes plain を; the contrasted object in the negative sentence takes は.

exercises.q: は can replace を to contrast or emphasize the object.
exercises.explain: Contrastive は overrides を and が and often follows other particles too.

exercises.answer: 私 は お茶 が 好き です

exercises.q: What does 私のです。mean?
exercises.explain: の after 私 stands for the possessed thing: 'the one of mine'.

sections.title: Particles of place, time and means
sections.summary: Beyond the core particles, Japanese uses に, で, へ, と, も, から and まで to express where, when, how and with whom something happens. This chapter sorts out the two 'at' particles に and で and the other everyday particles.

rules.title: に: location of existence and destination
rules.body: に marks the place where something exists or stays (with あります, います, 住んでいます) and the destination of movement verbs (行く, 来る, 帰る, 入る): 東京に住んでいます, 学校に行きます. Think of に as a pin on the map: the point where something is or ends up.

examples.target: 机の上に本があります。
examples.roman: Tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu.
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

rules.title: に: points in time
rules.body: に also marks a specific point in time: 七時に (at seven), 月曜日に (on Monday), 三月に (in March), 2020年に (in 2020). Relative time words that are not clock or calendar names (今日 today, 明日 tomorrow, 毎日 every day, 今週 this week, 今 now) take no particle at all.

examples.target: 月曜日に会いましょう。

examples.en: I'm going to Tokyo tomorrow. (no particle after 明日)

rules.title: で: place where an action happens
rules.body: で marks the place where an action takes place: 図書館で勉強します (study at the library), レストランで食べます (eat at a restaurant), 公園でサッカーをします. Contrast with に: 図書館にいます (I am at the library, existence) but 図書館で読みます (I read at the library, action).

examples.target: 公園でサッカーをします。
examples.en: I play soccer in the park.
I am at the library. (existence, so に)

rules.title: で: means, instrument and material
rules.body: で also marks the means by which something is done: a vehicle (バスで by bus), a tool (箸で with chopsticks), a language (日本語で in Japanese) or a material (木で out of wood). Going on foot is 歩いて, with no で.

examples.target: 日本語で話してください。

rules.title: へ: direction
rules.body: へ (pronounced e) marks the direction of movement and is largely interchangeable with に after 行く, 来る and 帰る: 日本へ行きます. へ stresses the direction of travel, に the arrival point; in everyday speech に is more common. Only へ can be followed by の: 東京への電車 (the train to Tokyo).

rules.title: と: 'and' between nouns, 'with' a person
rules.body: と joins nouns in a complete list (パンと牛乳 bread and milk) and marks the person you do something with (友達と映画を見ます). It cannot join verbs or adjectives; for a partial list ('things like A and B') や is used instead. 一緒に (together) often accompanies と.

examples.target: パンと牛乳を買います。

examples.en: I watch a film with a friend.

examples.target: 家族と一緒に住んでいます。
examples.roman: Kazoku to issho ni sunde imasu.
examples.en: I live together with my family.

rules.title: も: 'also, too'
rules.body: も means 'also' and replaces は, が or を: 私も学生です (I am also a student), 寿司も食べます (I eat sushi too). After other particles it is added rather than replacing them: 東京にも行きます (I'm going to Tokyo as well). With a negative verb も means 'neither / not ... either'.

examples.en: I'm going to Tokyo as well.

rules.title: から and まで: from and until
rules.body: から means 'from' and まで 'until, as far as', for both time and place: 九時から五時まで (from nine to five), 駅から家まで (from the station to home). They can be used singly: 明日から (from tomorrow), 東京まで (as far as Tokyo). からの and までの link them to nouns: 東京からの手紙 (a letter from Tokyo).

examples.target: 九時から五時まで働きます。
examples.en: I work from nine to five.

examples.target: 駅から家まで歩きます。
examples.en: I walk from the station to home.

rules.title: に: the receiver of giving and communicating
rules.body: に also marks the person something is given, sent or said to: 友達に手紙を書きます (write a letter to a friend), 母にプレゼントをあげます (give mother a present), 先生に聞きます (ask the teacher). The order is usually receiver に, then object を, then verb.

examples.target: 友達に手紙を書きます。
examples.en: I write a letter to a friend.

examples.target: 母にプレゼントをあげます。
examples.en: I give my mother a present.

exercises.q: 図書館___勉強します。(I study at the library.)
exercises.explain: で marks the place where an action happens.

exercises.q: 東京___住んでいます。(I live in Tokyo.)
exercises.explain: Living somewhere is a state of existence, so the place takes に.

exercises.q: に marks the place where an action such as studying or eating happens.
exercises.explain: That is で; に marks where something exists or where movement ends.

pairs: location of existence, destination, point in time

exercises.answer: 私 は 学校 に 行きます

exercises.q: バス___行きます。(I go by bus.)
exercises.explain: で marks the means of transport.

exercises.q: 七時___起きます。(I get up at seven.)
exercises.explain: Clock times are points in time and take に.

exercises.q: 明日に行きます is the correct way to say 'I'll go tomorrow'.
exercises.explain: Relative time words like 明日 take no particle: 明日行きます.

exercises.q: 私___学生です。(I am also a student.)
exercises.explain: も means 'also' and replaces は.

exercises.answer: 友達 と 映画 を 見ます
exercises.en: I watch a film with a friend.

exercises.q: 九時___五時まで働きます。(from nine)
exercises.explain: から marks the starting point and pairs with まで.

exercises.q: 日本語___話してください。(Please speak in Japanese.)
exercises.explain: The language used is a means, marked with で.

exercises.q: The direction particle へ is pronounced e.
exercises.explain: Like は and を, the particle へ has a special reading.

exercises.q: 猫が部屋___います。(There is a cat in the room.)
exercises.explain: With います the location takes に.

exercises.answer: 駅 から 家 まで 歩きます
exercises.en: I walk from the station to home.

exercises.q: パン___牛乳を買います。(I buy bread and milk.)
exercises.explain: と joins two nouns in a complete list.

exercises.q: 友達___手紙を書きます。(I write a letter to a friend.)
exercises.explain: The receiver of a letter is marked with に.

exercises.q: も replaces は, が or を rather than being added after them.
exercises.explain: 私も, not 私はも; after に or で it is added: 東京にも.

exercises.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I eat sushi too'?
exercises.explain: も takes the place of を directly after the noun.

exercises.answer: 毎日 電車 で 会社 へ 行きます
exercises.en: Every day I go to the office by train.

exercises.q: 日曜日___何をしますか。(on Sunday; time particle)
exercises.explain: Days of the week are calendar points and take に.

exercises.q: 友達とレストランで食べます means 'I eat at a restaurant with a friend'.
exercises.explain: と marks the companion and で the place of the action.

exercises.q: 水曜日から金曜日___休みです。(I'm off from Wednesday to Friday.)
exercises.explain: まで marks the end point of a span that started with から.

exercises.q: 公園___サッカーをします。(place of action)
exercises.explain: Playing is an action, so the park takes で.

exercises.answer: 田中さん も 東京 に 住んでいます
exercises.en: Mr Tanaka also lives in Tokyo.

exercises.q: 箸___食べます。(I eat with chopsticks.)
exercises.explain: A tool or instrument is marked with で; と is for a companion.

sections.title: です/ます politeness and sentence endings
sections.summary: Every Japanese sentence is spoken in either plain or polite style, and the choice is made at the end of the sentence. This chapter introduces the polite copula です, the polite verb ending ます, the question particle か and the sentence-final particles ね and よ.

rules.title: Plain style and polite style
rules.body: Japanese has two basic speech styles. The polite style ends sentences in です or 〜ます and is used with strangers, superiors, in shops and in most learning materials. The plain style ends in だ or the dictionary form of the verb and is used with family and close friends, and inside longer sentences. The style is chosen once per sentence, at the end.

examples.target: おいしいです。 / おいしい。

rules.title: Noun + です: the polite copula
rules.body: です links a noun (or adjective) to its topic: 私は学生です (I am a student). It covers English am, is and are and does not change for person or number. The polite negative is じゃありません (or the more formal ではありません); the plain equivalents are だ and じゃない. After an i-adjective です only adds politeness, and after a noun or na-adjective it is required.

examples.target: 田中さんは先生じゃありません。
examples.en: Mr Tanaka is not a teacher.

examples.target: ここは駅ではありません。
examples.roman: Koko wa eki de wa arimasen.

rules.title: Verb + ます: the polite verb ending
rules.body: Verbs in the polite style end in ます: 食べます (eat), 行きます (go), します (do). The ます form is used for present habits and for the future, since Japanese has no separate future tense: 明日行きます means 'I will go tomorrow'. The dictionary (plain) form is the one listed in dictionaries: 食べる, 行く, する.

examples.target: 毎日日本語を勉強します。

examples.en: I will go to Tokyo tomorrow.

rules.title: Questions with か
rules.body: To ask a yes/no question, simply add か to the end of a polite sentence; the word order does not change and the voice rises slightly: 学生ですか (Are you a student?). A question mark is optional in Japanese writing because か already marks the question. Question-word questions work the same way: 何ですか (What is it?).

examples.target: コーヒーを飲みますか。

rules.title: Answering yes and no
rules.body: Yes is はい, no is いいえ. A full answer repeats the predicate: はい、学生です (Yes, I am a student), いいえ、学生じゃありません. The set phrases はい、そうです (yes, that's right) and いいえ、違います (no, that's wrong) are used for noun sentences. Note that to a negative question はい agrees with the statement, so 'はい' can mean 'no, I don't'.

rules.title: ね: seeking agreement
rules.body: The particle ね at the end of a sentence invites the listener to agree or confirms shared knowledge, like English 'isn't it?', 'right?': いい天気ですね (Nice weather, isn't it?). It softens statements and keeps the conversation friendly. With a falling tone it can also express mild emphasis.

examples.en: Tomorrow is a day off, right?

rules.title: よ: giving new information
rules.body: The particle よ marks the sentence as information the listener does not have, like 'you know' or 'I tell you': この店はおいしいですよ (This restaurant is good, you know). It adds assurance or a light warning. よ and ね can combine as よね when you are fairly sure but want confirmation.

examples.target: この店はおいしいですよ。
examples.roman: Kono mise wa oishii desu yo.
examples.en: This restaurant is good, you know.
The bus has come (I'm telling you).

examples.roman: Ashita wa yasumi desu yo ne.
examples.en: Tomorrow is a day off, right?

rules.title: Dropping the subject
rules.body: Japanese leaves out any noun that is clear from context, including I and you. 学生です can mean 'I am a student' or 'she is a student' depending on the situation, and 行きますか — 行きます is a complete exchange. Over-using 私 and especially あなた sounds unnatural; address people by name plus さん instead.

examples.target: 学生ですか。— はい、学生です。
examples.roman: Gakusei desu ka. — Hai, gakusei desu.
examples.en: Are you a student? — Yes, I am.

examples.target: 明日行きますか。— 行きます。
examples.en: Are you going tomorrow? — I am.

examples.target: 田中さんは行きますか。
examples.en: Are you going, Mr Tanaka? (name instead of 'you')

rules.title: Names and さん
rules.body: さん is attached to other people's family or given names: 田中さん (Mr/Ms Tanaka), 山田さんは (as for Ms Yamada). It is never used for yourself or your own family members when speaking to outsiders. Professions can serve as titles: 先生 (teacher, doctor). In casual speech plain forms such as だ and the dictionary form replace です and ます, and questions are made with a rising tone alone: 行く？

examples.en: I am Tanaka. (no さん for yourself)

exercises.q: The polite form of 'I am a student':
exercises.explain: Nouns take the polite copula です; だ is the plain form.

exercises.q: 私は先生___。(polite copula)
exercises.explain: です links the noun 先生 politely to the topic.

exercises.q: Adding か to the end of a polite sentence turns it into a question.
exercises.explain: Word order stays the same; か alone marks the question.

exercises.answer: あなた は 学生 です か

exercises.q: The polite form of 食べる (to eat):
exercises.explain: Ru-verbs drop る and add ます.

exercises.q: いい天気です___。(Nice weather, isn't it?)
exercises.explain: ね seeks the listener's agreement.

exercises.q: In Japanese questions the word order changes, as in English.
exercises.explain: Japanese keeps the statement order and adds か at the end.

exercises.q: Which ending tells the listener something they did not know?
exercises.explain: よ asserts new information; ね seeks agreement.

exercises.answer: 田中さん は 先生 じゃ ありません
exercises.en: Mr Tanaka is not a teacher.

exercises.q: はい、そう___。(Yes, that's right. polite)
exercises.explain: そうです is the set polite answer confirming a noun sentence.

exercises.q: The plain (dictionary) form of 行きます:
exercises.explain: 行く is the form listed in dictionaries and used in plain speech.

exercises.q: You add さん to your own name when introducing yourself.
exercises.explain: さん honours other people and is never used for yourself.

exercises.q: 田中___は先生です。(polite title after a name)
exercises.explain: さん is the neutral polite title for other people.

exercises.answer: 私 は 毎日 日本語 を 勉強します

exercises.q: How do you reply 'No, that's wrong'?
exercises.explain: いいえ is 'no' and 違います means 'it is different / wrong'.

exercises.q: Subjects are often dropped when clear from context, so 学生です can mean 'I am a student'.
exercises.explain: Japanese omits pronouns that context supplies.

exercises.q: 明日は休み___か。(Is tomorrow a day off? polite)
exercises.explain: A polite noun question is noun + です + か.

exercises.q: Which is the appropriate way to ask a stranger where the station is?
options: すみません、駅はどこですか。
exercises.explain: Strangers are addressed in the polite style with です and か.

exercises.answer: これ は おいしい です よ

exercises.q: What is the plain equivalent of です?
exercises.explain: だ is the plain copula used with friends and family.

exercises.q: ではありません is a more formal version of じゃありません.
exercises.explain: じゃ is a contraction of では and sounds more conversational.

exercises.q: 学生___ありません。(not a student; conversational polite negative)
exercises.explain: じゃありません is the everyday polite negative of です.

exercises.answer: 明日 は 雨 です ね
exercises.en: It's going to rain tomorrow, isn't it?

exercises.q: A friend asks 行く？ with rising intonation. This is:
exercises.explain: In plain style a rising tone alone makes a question; no か or ます is needed.

exercises.q: ね is used to push new information on the listener, and よ seeks agreement.
exercises.explain: It is the other way round: よ gives information, ね seeks agreement.

sections.title: Verb groups and the te-form
sections.summary: Japanese verbs fall into three groups, and knowing the group tells you how to conjugate. This chapter teaches the groups, the ます stem and the all-purpose te-form, used for ongoing actions (〜ています), requests (〜てください) and linking actions.

rules.title: Three verb groups
rules.body: Group 1 verbs (u-verbs, godan) end in an u-sound in the dictionary form: 書く kaku, 飲む nomu, 話す hanasu, 買う kau, 待つ matsu. Group 2 verbs (ru-verbs, ichidan) end in -iru or -eru: 食べる taberu, 見る miru, 起きる okiru. There are only two irregular verbs: する (do) and 来る (come). Compound verbs like 勉強する follow する.

examples.target: 食べる・見る・起きる

rules.title: Spotting ru-verbs and the exceptions
rules.body: A verb is a ru-verb only if it ends in -iru or -eru; verbs like 読む or 話す that do not end in る are always u-verbs. Some verbs end in -iru/-eru but are still u-verbs and must be memorized: 帰る (return), 知る (know), 走る (run), 入る (enter), 切る (cut), 要る (need), 喋る (chat). Their ます forms show it: 帰ります, not 帰ます.

rules.title: The ます stem
rules.body: U-verbs change the final u-sound to the i-sound and add ます: 書く → 書きます, 飲む → 飲みます, 話す → 話します, 買う → 買います, 待つ → 待ちます. Ru-verbs simply drop る: 食べる → 食べます, 見る → 見ます. The irregulars are する → します and 来る → 来ます (kimasu). The part before ます is the stem, also used with 〜たい and 〜ましょう.

rules.title: Te-form of ru-verbs and irregular verbs
rules.body: Ru-verbs form the te-form by replacing る with て: 食べる → 食べて, 見る → 見て, 起きる → 起きて. The irregulars are する → して and 来る → 来て (kite). The te-form never stands alone as a complete polite sentence; it connects to what follows.

rules.title: Te-form of u-verbs
rules.body: The ending decides the te-form. う, つ, る → って (買う → 買って, 待つ → 待って, 帰る → 帰って); む, ぶ, ぬ → んで (飲む → 飲んで, 遊ぶ → 遊んで, 死ぬ → 死んで); く → いて (書く → 書いて) but ぐ → いで (泳ぐ → 泳いで); す → して (話す → 話して). The one exception is 行く (go) → 行って, not 行いて.

examples.target: 書く → 書いて / 泳ぐ → 泳いで

rules.title: 〜ています: ongoing action and resulting state
rules.body: Te-form + います expresses an action in progress: 今テレビを見ています (I am watching TV now), or a habit continuing over time: 毎日勉強しています. With verbs that describe a change, it expresses the state that results: 結婚しています (is married), 住んでいます (lives), 知っています (knows), 持っています (has). The negative is 〜ていません, which also means 'has not yet' with まだ.

examples.target: 今テレビを見ています。
田中さんを知っていますか。

rules.title: 〜てください: polite requests
rules.body: Te-form + ください makes a polite request or instruction: ちょっと待ってください (Please wait a moment), 名前を書いてください (Please write your name). It is suitable for shops, classrooms and asking for help. Dropping ください (待って) gives a casual request among friends. For 'please don't', the negative form 〜ないでください is used.

examples.target: ちょっと待ってください。
名前を書いてください。
もう一度言ってください。

rules.title: Linking actions with the te-form
rules.body: The te-form joins actions in sequence, like 'and then': 朝起きて、コーヒーを飲んで、会社に行きます. Only the last verb carries the tense and politeness, so the whole chain is polite present here. The te-form can also give the manner or reason: 歩いて行きます (go on foot), 風邪をひいて休みました (I caught a cold and took the day off).

examples.target: 朝起きて、コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.en: I get up in the morning and drink coffee.

examples.target: 図書館に行って、本を読みました。
examples.roman: Toshokan ni itte, hon o yomimashita.
examples.en: I went to the library and read a book.

rules.title: 〜てもいいですか: asking permission
rules.body: Te-form + もいいですか asks for permission: 写真を撮ってもいいですか (May I take a photo?). The answer はい、いいですよ grants it; the refusal is usually softened, for example すみません、ちょっと… Te-form + はいけません states a prohibition: ここで食べてはいけません.

examples.target: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.roman: Shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.

examples.target: ここで食べてはいけません。

exercises.q: Which group does 食べる belong to?
exercises.explain: It ends in -eru and conjugates by dropping る: 食べます, 食べて.

exercises.q: 書く → te-form: ___ (kaite)
exercises.explain: U-verbs ending in く change く to いて.

exercises.q: 行く has the irregular te-form 行って.
exercises.explain: By the く rule it would be 行いて, but 行く is the one exception.

exercises.answer: ちょっと 待って ください

exercises.q: The te-form of する:
exercises.explain: する is irregular: します, して.

exercises.q: 来る → te-form: ___ (kite)
exercises.explain: 来る is irregular; its stem changes to き in 来ます and 来て.

exercises.q: 帰る (to return) is a ru-verb because it ends in -eru.
exercises.explain: 帰る is an exception: it is a u-verb, 帰ります and 帰って.

exercises.q: The ます form of 読む (to read):
exercises.explain: U-verbs change the final u-sound to i before ます: mu → mi.

exercises.answer: 今 テレビ を 見て います

exercises.q: 東京に住んで___。(I live in Tokyo; ongoing state, polite)
exercises.explain: 住む in 〜ています expresses the continuing state of living somewhere.

exercises.q: The te-form of 泳ぐ (to swim):
exercises.explain: ぐ becomes いで, the voiced counterpart of く → いて.

exercises.q: 〜ています can express a resulting state, as in 結婚しています 'is married'.
exercises.explain: With change-of-state verbs 〜ている describes the state after the change.

exercises.q: 名前を書いて___。(Please write your name.)
exercises.explain: Te-form + ください makes a polite request.

exercises.answer: 朝 起きて コーヒー を 飲みます
exercises.en: I get up in the morning and drink coffee.

exercises.q: The te-form of 待つ (to wait):
exercises.explain: つ belongs to the う・つ・る group, which takes って.

exercises.q: 死ぬ → te-form: ___ (shinde)
exercises.explain: ぬ belongs with む and ぶ, which take んで.

exercises.q: Ru-verbs form the polite form by dropping る and adding ます: 見る → 見ます.
exercises.explain: Ru-verbs keep the whole stem and only replace る.

exercises.q: Which verb is irregular?
exercises.explain: 来る and する are the only irregular verbs; its stem changes to き and こ.

exercises.answer: 窓 を 開けて ください

exercises.q: 話す → te-form: ___ (hanashite)
exercises.explain: Verbs ending in す take して.

exercises.q: What does 知っていますか mean?
exercises.explain: 知る in 〜ている expresses the state of knowing.

exercises.q: 入る (to enter) is a u-verb: 入ります, 入って.
exercises.explain: Despite ending in -iru, 入る is one of the exceptional u-verbs.

exercises.q: 遊ぶ → te-form: ___ (asonde)
exercises.explain: ぶ takes んで, like む and ぬ.

exercises.answer: ここ で 写真 を 撮って も いい です か

exercises.q: 毎日日本語を勉強しています。describes:
exercises.explain: 〜ています with 毎日 expresses an activity that continues over time.

exercises.q: The te-form can link two actions in sequence, with only the last verb showing tense.
exercises.explain: 起きて、飲みます: the final ます carries politeness and tense for both.

sections.title: Negative and past forms
sections.summary: Japanese verbs and adjectives change their endings for negative and past, in both polite and plain style. This chapter gives the four-way pattern (present, negative, past, past negative) for verbs, i-adjectives, na-adjectives and nouns.

rules.title: Polite verb forms: ません, ました, ませんでした
rules.body: In the polite style the ます ending changes: 〜ます (present/future), 〜ません (negative), 〜ました (past), 〜ませんでした (past negative). The stem never changes: 食べます, 食べません, 食べました, 食べませんでした. The same endings apply to all three verb groups: します, しません, しました; 来ます, 来ません, 来ました.

examples.target: 昨日は学校に行きませんでした。
examples.roman: Kinō wa gakkō ni ikimasen deshita.
examples.en: I didn't go to school yesterday.

rules.title: Plain negative 〜ない
rules.body: Ru-verbs drop る and add ない: 食べる → 食べない, 見る → 見ない. U-verbs change the final u-sound to the a-sound and add ない: 書く → 書かない, 飲む → 飲まない, 話す → 話さない, 待つ → 待たない; verbs ending in う take わ: 買う → 買わない. Irregulars: する → しない, 来る → 来ない (konai). The negative of ある is simply ない.

rules.title: Plain past 〜た
rules.body: The plain past is made exactly like the te-form, with た/だ instead of て/で: 食べて → 食べた, 書いて → 書いた, 飲んで → 飲んだ, 買って → 買った, 話して → 話した, して → した, 来て → 来た (kita), 行って → 行った. It is used in casual speech and inside longer sentences.

examples.en: I ate sushi with a friend.

rules.title: Plain past negative 〜なかった
rules.body: The plain past negative is formed from the ない form by replacing い with かった: 食べない → 食べなかった, 書かない → 書かなかった, しない → しなかった, 来ない → 来なかった. ない itself behaves like an i-adjective, which is why its past is かった.

examples.target: 昨日は何も食べなかった。
行く → 行かない → 行かなかった

rules.title: Negative and past of i-adjectives
rules.body: I-adjectives drop the final い and add くない (negative), かった (past) or くなかった (past negative): 高い → 高くない, 高かった, 高くなかった. いい (good) uses the stem よ: よくない, よかった, よくなかった. In the polite style です is simply added after each form: 高くないです, 高かったです. Never say 高いでした or 高いじゃない.

examples.target: 映画はおもしろくなかった。

rules.title: Negative and past of nouns and na-adjectives
rules.body: Nouns and na-adjectives use the copula: polite です, じゃありません, でした, じゃありませんでした; plain だ, じゃない, だった, じゃなかった. 学生です → 学生でした (was a student), 静かです → 静かじゃありません (is not quiet), 元気だった (was well). ではありません and ではなかった are the formal versions of じゃ.

examples.target: 来週は暇じゃありません。
昨日は元気じゃなかった。

rules.title: Time words that go with the past
rules.body: The past tense is typically accompanied by time words such as 昨日 (yesterday), 先週 (last week), 先月 (last month), 去年 (last year), さっき (a moment ago). もう (already) goes with the past: もう食べました (I have already eaten). まだ (still, not yet) goes with the negative 〜ていません: まだ食べていません (I haven't eaten yet), not with ませんでした.

examples.target: 先週、京都に行きました。
examples.en: I went to Kyoto last week.
I have already done the homework.

rules.title: The full pattern side by side
rules.body: For every predicate you need four forms in two styles. Verb (polite): 行きます, 行きません, 行きました, 行きませんでした; (plain): 行く, 行かない, 行った, 行かなかった. I-adjective: 高いです, 高くないです, 高かったです, 高くなかったです. Noun or na-adjective: 元気です, 元気じゃありません, 元気でした, 元気じゃありませんでした. Only the ending changes; the words before it stay the same.

examples.target: 行きます・行きません・行きました・行きませんでした
examples.en: go, don't go, went, didn't go (polite)

examples.target: 高い・高くない・高かった・高くなかった
examples.en: expensive, not expensive, was expensive, wasn't expensive

examples.target: 元気だ・元気じゃない・元気だった・元気じゃなかった
examples.roman: genki da, genki ja nai, genki datta, genki ja nakatta
examples.en: well, not well, was well, wasn't well (plain)

exercises.q: The polite negative of 食べます:
exercises.explain: ます becomes ません in the polite negative.

exercises.q: 昨日、映画を見___。(polite past)
exercises.explain: ます becomes ました for the polite past.

exercises.q: 〜ませんでした is the polite past negative.
exercises.explain: ません plus でした puts the negative into the past.

exercises.answer: 昨日 は 学校 に 行きません でした
exercises.en: I didn't go to school yesterday.

exercises.q: The plain negative of 飲む:
exercises.explain: U-verbs change the final u-sound to a before ない: mu → ma.

exercises.q: 買う → plain negative: ___ (kawanai)
exercises.explain: Verbs ending in う take わ, not あ, before ない.

exercises.q: The plain negative of ある is あらない.
exercises.explain: ある is exceptional: its plain negative is simply ない.

exercises.q: The plain past of 書く:
exercises.explain: The plain past follows the te-form rule: 書いて → 書いた.

exercises.answer: 友達 と 寿司 を 食べた
exercises.en: I ate sushi with a friend.

exercises.q: 高い → negative: ___ (takakunai)
exercises.explain: I-adjectives replace い with くない.

exercises.q: The past of いい (good):
exercises.explain: いい conjugates on the stem よ: よくない, よかった.

exercises.q: The past of an i-adjective is formed by replacing い with かった.
exercises.explain: 高い → 高かった, おいしい → おいしかった.

exercises.q: 昨日は寒___です。(It was cold yesterday; polite)
exercises.explain: The past かった form takes です for politeness.

exercises.answer: 来週 は 暇 じゃ ありません

exercises.q: What does 学生でした mean?
exercises.explain: でした is the polite past of です.

exercises.q: 静か → plain negative: ___ (shizuka ja nai)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives use the copula's negative じゃない.

exercises.q: 来る has the plain negative 来ない, read konai.
exercises.explain: The irregular 来る changes its stem vowel to こ in the negative.

exercises.q: The plain past of する:
exercises.explain: する is irregular: して, した.

exercises.answer: もう 宿題 を しました
exercises.en: I have already done the homework.

exercises.q: まだ食べて___。(I haven't eaten yet; polite)
exercises.explain: 'Not yet' is まだ + 〜ていません, not ませんでした.

exercises.q: The plain past negative of 行く:
exercises.explain: 行かない → 行かなかった: ない changes to なかった.

exercises.q: おいしいじゃない is the correct negative of おいしい.
exercises.explain: I-adjectives take くない: おいしくない.

exercises.q: 元気___。(I was well; polite past of a na-adjective)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives and nouns use でした for the polite past.

exercises.answer: 昨日 の 映画 は おもしろく なかった

exercises.q: The plain past of 飲む:
exercises.explain: む takes んだ, parallel to the te-form んで.

exercises.q: 来ませんでした means 'did not come'.
exercises.explain: ませんでした is the polite past negative ending.

sections.title: i-adjectives and na-adjectives
sections.summary: Japanese adjectives come in two kinds, i-adjectives and na-adjectives, which differ in how they attach to nouns, how they negate and how they link to other adjectives. This chapter covers both, plus adverbs and 'becoming'.

rules.title: Two kinds of adjectives
rules.body: I-adjectives end in い in their dictionary form: 高い (expensive, tall), おいしい (delicious), 新しい (new), 大きい (big). Na-adjectives do not conjugate like that and need な before a noun: 静か (quiet), 元気 (well, lively), 有名 (famous), 便利 (convenient), 親切 (kind). A few na-adjectives happen to end in い and must be memorized: きれい (pretty, clean) and 嫌い (disliked).

examples.target: 高い・おいしい・新しい

examples.en: pretty / clean, disliked (na-adjectives ending in い)

rules.title: Before a noun
rules.body: An i-adjective goes directly before the noun: 高い山 (a tall mountain), 新しい車 (a new car). A na-adjective takes な: 静かな町 (a quiet town), 有名なレストラン (a famous restaurant), きれいな花 (a pretty flower). Never put な after an i-adjective.

rules.title: At the end of a sentence
rules.body: As a predicate, an i-adjective stands on its own in plain style and takes です for politeness: 高い / 高いです. A na-adjective needs the copula: 静かだ (plain) / 静かです (polite); な is not used here. The topic is marked with は: この店は高いです, この町は静かです.

rules.title: Negative forms
rules.body: I-adjectives: drop い, add くない (plain) or くないです / くありません (polite): 高くない, 高くないです. いい becomes よくない. Na-adjectives: add じゃない (plain) or じゃありません (polite): 静かじゃない, 静かじゃありません. The common mistake is 高いじゃない, which is wrong.

examples.target: このカレーは辛くないです。

rules.title: Past forms
rules.body: I-adjectives: drop い, add かった (plain) or かったです (polite): おいしかった, おいしかったです; いい → よかった. Na-adjectives use the copula's past: 静かだった (plain), 静かでした (polite). Past negatives are 高くなかった(です) and 静かじゃなかった / 静かじゃありませんでした.

examples.target: 昨日は天気がよかったです。
examples.roman: Kinō wa tenki ga yokatta desu.

examples.target: パーティーはにぎやかでした。

rules.title: Linking adjectives: 〜くて and 〜で
rules.body: To say 'A and B' with adjectives, put the first in its linking form. I-adjectives drop い and add くて: 安くておいしい (cheap and delicious), 大きくて新しい. Na-adjectives (and nouns) take で: 静かできれい (quiet and pretty), 親切でおもしろい人. Only the last adjective shows tense and politeness.

examples.target: この店は安くておいしいです。
examples.roman: Kono mise wa yasukute oishii desu.
examples.en: This shop is cheap and delicious.

examples.target: 東京は大きくてにぎやかです。
田中さんは親切でおもしろい人です。
examples.roman: Tanaka-san wa shinsetsu de omoshiroi hito desu.
examples.en: Mr Tanaka is a kind and funny person.

rules.title: Adverbs from adjectives
rules.body: An i-adjective becomes an adverb by changing い to く: 早い → 早く (early, quickly), 大きい → 大きく (loudly, big). A na-adjective becomes an adverb with に: 静か → 静かに (quietly), 上手 → 上手に (skilfully). いい → よく (well, often).

examples.target: 静かに話してください。

rules.title: Becoming: 〜くなる and 〜になる
rules.body: The adverb form plus なる (to become) expresses change: 寒くなりました (it has become cold), 大きくなる (grow big); 静かになる (become quiet), きれいになりました (has become clean). Nouns also take になる: 先生になりたいです (I want to become a teacher). いい → よくなる (get better).

examples.target: 部屋がきれいになりました。
日本語が上手になりました。

rules.title: Degree words: とても, あまり, ちょっと
rules.body: とても (very) and すごく (really) strengthen an adjective: とても高いです. あまり (not very) is used only with a negative: あまり高くないです. ちょっと (a bit) softens: ちょっと高いです, and 全然 (not at all) also requires a negative: 全然おもしろくない.

examples.target: あまりおもしろくないです。

exercises.q: Which of these is a na-adjective?
exercises.explain: 静か needs な before a noun: 静かな町; the others end in い and conjugate.

exercises.q: 静か___町 (a quiet town)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives take な before a noun.

exercises.q: きれい is an i-adjective because it ends in い.
exercises.explain: きれい is a na-adjective: きれいな花, きれいじゃない.

exercises.answer: この 店 は 安くて おいしい です
exercises.en: This shop is cheap and delicious.

exercises.q: The negative of 高い:
exercises.explain: I-adjectives replace い with くない.

exercises.q: 元気___ありません。(I'm not well; polite)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives negate with じゃありません.

exercises.q: Two i-adjectives are linked with 〜くて: 大きくて新しい.
exercises.explain: The first i-adjective drops い and takes くて.

exercises.q: 'a famous restaurant':
exercises.explain: 有名 is a na-adjective, so it takes な before the noun.

exercises.answer: 田中さん は 親切 で おもしろい 人 です
exercises.en: Mr Tanaka is a kind and funny person.

exercises.q: 早___起きます。(I get up early; adverb)
exercises.explain: I-adjectives form adverbs by changing い to く.

exercises.q: The past of おいしい:
exercises.explain: I-adjectives replace い with かった; でした is not used after them.

exercises.q: いい becomes よくない in the negative.
exercises.explain: いい conjugates on the older stem よ.

exercises.q: 部屋がきれい___なりました。(The room has become clean.)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives take に before なる.

exercises.answer: この 本 は あまり おもしろく ない です
exercises.en: This book is not very interesting.

exercises.q: あまり (not very) is used together with:
exercises.explain: あまり needs a negative: あまり高くない.

exercises.q: 寒___なりました。(It has become cold.)
exercises.explain: I-adjectives take the く form before なる.

exercises.q: Before a noun, i-adjectives take な: 高いな山.
exercises.explain: I-adjectives attach directly: 高い山; only na-adjectives take な.

exercises.q: The plain past negative of 静か:
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives use the copula: じゃない → じゃなかった.

exercises.answer: 東京 は 大きくて にぎやか です

exercises.q: 静か___話してください。(Please speak quietly.)
exercises.explain: Na-adjectives form adverbs with に.

exercises.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: このカレーは辛くないです
このカレーは辛いじゃないです
このカレーは辛いくないです
このカレーは辛ないです
exercises.explain: 辛い is an i-adjective: drop い, add くない.

exercises.q: 好き and 嫌い are na-adjectives: 好きな食べ物.
exercises.explain: Both take な before a noun and じゃない in the negative.

exercises.q: 昨日は天気がよ___です。(The weather was good yesterday.)
exercises.explain: いい uses the stem よ: よかった.

exercises.answer: 新しい 車 は とても 高い です
exercises.en: The new car is very expensive.

exercises.q: What does ちょっと高いです mean?
exercises.explain: ちょっと means 'a little' and softens the statement.

exercises.q: 便利 (convenient) is a na-adjective: 便利な店.
exercises.explain: 便利 does not end in い and takes な before a noun.

sections.title: Existence and possession
sections.summary: Japanese says 'there is' and 'I have' with two verbs, あります for things and います for living beings. This chapter covers the pattern 場所に〜があります, position words, and the basics of counting with counters.

rules.title: あります and います
rules.body: あります (plain ある) expresses the existence of inanimate things, plants and abstract things: 本があります (there is a book), 時間があります (there is time). います (plain いる) is for people and animals: 猫がいます (there is a cat), 学生がいます. The negatives are ありません / いません, the past forms ありました / いました. Plants take あります even though they are alive.

examples.en: There is no time. / I have no time.

rules.title: The pattern 場所に 物が あります
rules.body: To say where something is, use place + に, then the thing + が, then the verb: 部屋にテレビがあります (There is a TV in the room), 公園に子供がいます (There are children in the park). To say where a known thing is, make it the topic: テレビは部屋にあります (The TV is in the room), 田中さんは東京にいます.

examples.target: 部屋にテレビがあります。
examples.en: There is a TV in the room.
There are children in the park.

examples.target: トイレはどこにありますか。
examples.roman: Toire wa doko ni arimasu ka.

rules.title: Possession: 〜があります / 〜がいます
rules.body: Japanese has no everyday verb 'to have'; instead you say that something exists with respect to you: 私は車があります (I have a car), 兄がいます (I have an older brother), 時間がありません (I have no time). The possessor is the topic with は and the thing possessed takes が. 持っています (is holding, has) is used for things you carry or own.

examples.en: I don't have a younger sister.

rules.title: Position words
rules.body: Relative positions are nouns joined with の: 机の上 (on the desk), 机の下 (under the desk), かばんの中 (in the bag), 駅の前 (in front of the station), 家の後ろ (behind the house), 銀行の隣 (next to the bank), 駅の近く (near the station). These phrases then take に: 机の上に本があります.

examples.target: 机の上に本があります。
examples.roman: Tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu.
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

examples.target: 駅は銀行の前にあります。
examples.roman: Eki wa ginkō no mae ni arimasu.
examples.en: The station is in front of the bank.

examples.target: かばんの中に何がありますか。
examples.roman: Kaban no naka ni nani ga arimasu ka.

rules.title: Nobody and nothing: 誰も / 何も + negative
rules.body: Question word + も with a negative verb means 'no one', 'nothing', 'nowhere': 誰もいません (there is no one), 何もありません (there is nothing), どこにもありません (it is nowhere). Question word + か means 'someone / something': 誰かいますか (Is anyone there?).

examples.target: ここには誰もいません。
examples.roman: Koko ni wa dare mo imasen.

examples.target: 冷蔵庫に何もありません。
examples.en: There is nothing in the fridge.

rules.title: Counters: the basics
rules.body: Numbers are followed by a counter that depends on what is counted. The native set 一つ (hitotsu), 二つ (futatsu), 三つ (mittsu), 四つ (yottsu), 五つ (itsutsu), 六つ (muttsu), 七つ (nanatsu), 八つ (yattsu), 九つ (kokonotsu), とお (tō) counts general objects up to ten. People use 人: 一人 (hitori), 二人 (futari), then 三人 (sannin), 四人 (yonin). Other common counters are 本 (long things), 枚 (flat things), 匹 (small animals), 冊 (bound books), 台 (machines).

examples.target: りんごが三つあります。

rules.title: Sound changes with counters
rules.body: Some numbers change shape before certain counters. With 本 (hon): 一本 ippon, 三本 sanbon, 六本 roppon, 八本 happon, 十本 juppon, 何本 nanbon. With 匹 (hiki): 一匹 ippiki, 三匹 sanbiki, 六匹 roppiki. With 枚 (mai) there are no changes: 一枚 ichimai, 三枚 sanmai. With 冊 (satsu): 一冊 issatsu, 八冊 hassatsu. 四 is read よん and 七 なな before most counters.

examples.en: There are five sheets of paper.

rules.title: Where the counter goes
rules.body: The number plus counter normally comes after the noun and its particle, right before the verb: 猫が二匹います, ビールを三本ください. It can also go before the noun with の: 二匹の猫 (two cats), but the first order is more common in speech. To ask how many, use いくつ (general) or 何 + counter: 何人 (how many people), 何本, 何枚.

examples.target: ビールを三本ください。

rules.title: あります for events
rules.body: あります is also used for events and happenings: 会議があります (there is a meeting), 明日テストがあります (there is a test tomorrow), 今晩パーティーがあります. The place of an event takes で, not に, because the event is an action: 東京で会議があります.

examples.target: 明日テストがあります。
東京で会議があります。
examples.en: There is a meeting in Tokyo.

examples.target: 今晩パーティーがあります。

exercises.q: 猫が___。(There is a cat.)
exercises.explain: Animals and people take います.

exercises.q: 机の上に本が___。(There is a book on the desk; polite)
exercises.explain: Inanimate things exist with あります.

exercises.q: います is used for people and animals, あります for things.
exercises.explain: The choice depends on whether the thing is animate.

exercises.answer: 部屋 に テレビ が あります
exercises.en: There is a TV in the room.

exercises.q: 私は兄が___。(I have an older brother.)
exercises.explain: A brother is a person, so possession is expressed with います.

exercises.q: 本が二___あります。(two books; counter for bound books)
exercises.explain: 冊 counts books, magazines and notebooks.

exercises.q: 三人 is read さんにん.
exercises.explain: From three upward the people counter is a regular number + にん.

exercises.q: How is 一人 read?
exercises.explain: One and two people use native readings: ひとり, ふたり.

exercises.answer: 学生 が 三人 います

exercises.q: りんごが三___あります。(three apples; generic counter)
exercises.explain: The native counter 一つ, 二つ, 三つ counts general objects.

exercises.q: The negative of います:
exercises.explain: います follows the normal ます → ません pattern.

exercises.q: Plants take います because they are alive.
exercises.explain: Plants are treated as immobile things and take あります.

exercises.q: 駅は銀行の___にあります。(The station is in front of the bank.)
exercises.explain: Position words are nouns linked with の and followed by に.

exercises.answer: かばん の 中 に 何 が あります か

exercises.q: What does 時間がありません mean?
exercises.explain: ありません is the negative of あります; abstract things like time use あります.

exercises.q: 犬が___います。(There is one dog; number + counter for small animals, いっぴき)
exercises.explain: 一 + 匹 becomes いっぴき with a sound change.

exercises.q: 机の上に means 'on the desk'.
exercises.explain: 上 is the position noun 'top / above', linked to 机 with の.

exercises.q: The plain form of あります:
exercises.explain: ある is the dictionary form; いる is the plain form of います.

exercises.answer: ここ に は 誰 も いません

exercises.q: 紙が五___あります。(five sheets of paper; counter for flat things)
exercises.explain: 枚 counts flat objects such as paper, tickets and shirts.

exercises.q: Which sentence has the counter in its usual position: 'There are two cats'?
exercises.explain: Number + counter follows the noun and particle and precedes the verb.

exercises.q: 会議があります 'There is a meeting' uses あります even though a meeting is an event.
exercises.explain: Events and abstract things exist with あります.

exercises.q: 妹が___。(I don't have a younger sister; polite)
exercises.explain: A sister is a person, so the negative is いません.

exercises.answer: トイレ は どこ に あります か

exercises.q: In ペンが三本あります, how is 三本 read?
exercises.explain: After 三 the counter 本 is voiced to ぼん.

exercises.q: 八つ is read やっつ.
exercises.explain: The native numbers run ひとつ, ふたつ ... やっつ, ここのつ, とお.

sections.title: Demonstratives, questions and word order
sections.summary: This chapter covers the こ・そ・あ・ど system of pointing words, the question words 誰, 何, どこ and いつ, and the basic subject-object-verb order of Japanese, including when subjects are dropped.

rules.title: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
rules.body: Pronouns for things follow a three-way system based on distance. これ is something near the speaker (this), それ something near the listener (that), あれ something far from both (that over there), and どれ asks 'which one?'. They stand alone as nouns: これは何ですか (What is this?), それは私のです (That is mine).

examples.roman: Sore wa watashi no hon desu.

examples.en: That over there is Mount Fuji.

examples.target: どれがあなたのですか。
examples.roman: Dore ga anata no desu ka.

rules.title: この・その・あの・どの before nouns
rules.body: When a noun follows, use この, その, あの or どの instead: この本 (this book), その人 (that person near you), あの店 (that shop over there), どの電車 (which train). These forms never stand alone; they must be followed by a noun.

examples.roman: Kono hon wa watashi no desu.
Ano hito wa dare desu ka.
examples.en: Who is that person over there?

examples.target: どの電車に乗りますか。

rules.title: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ for places
rules.body: The same system applies to places: ここ (here), そこ (there, near you), あそこ (over there) and どこ (where). The polite direction words こちら, そちら, あちら, どちら are used for places, directions, people and 'which of two'. どちら is also a polite 'where': お国はどちらですか.

rules.title: The question words
rules.body: The basic question words are 誰 (who), 何 (what), どこ (where), いつ (when), どう (how), どうして / なぜ (why), いくら (how much, price), いくつ (how many, how old), どんな (what kind of) and どの / どれ (which). They take the same particle as the noun they replace: 誰が (who, subject), 何を (what, object), どこで (where, place of action).

examples.target: いつ日本に来ましたか。
examples.en: When did you come to Japan?

rules.title: なん and なに
rules.body: 何 is read なん before です, before た/だ/な sounds and before counters: 何ですか (nan desu ka), 何時 (nanji, what time), 何人 (nannin, how many people). It is read なに before particles such as を, が and も: 何を (nani o), 何が, 何も. Both appear in 何か (nanika, something).

rules.title: Questions keep the statement order
rules.body: A question word stays in the position of the word it replaces; nothing moves to the front. Compare 田中さんは東京で働いています (Tanaka works in Tokyo) with 田中さんはどこで働いていますか (Where does Tanaka work?). The only change is か at the end. Time, place and object keep their positions.

examples.target: 田中さんはどこで働いていますか。
examples.roman: Tanaka-san wa doko de hataraite imasu ka.

examples.target: あなたはいつ日本に来ましたか。
examples.roman: Anata wa itsu Nihon ni kimashita ka.
examples.en: When did you come to Japan?

rules.title: Basic word order: SOV
rules.body: Japanese is a subject-object-verb language: the verb (or です) always comes last. The usual order is topic/subject, time, place, object, verb: 私は毎日公園で走ります (I run in the park every day). Because particles mark each role, the elements before the verb can be rearranged for emphasis, but the verb stays at the end and modifiers come before what they modify.

examples.target: 私は毎日公園で走ります。
examples.roman: Watashi wa mainichi kōen de hashirimasu.
examples.en: I run in the park every day.

examples.target: 田中さんは昨日図書館で本を読みました。
examples.roman: Tanaka-san wa kinō toshokan de hon o yomimashita.
examples.en: Mr Tanaka read a book at the library yesterday.

examples.target: 毎日公園で私は走ります。
examples.roman: Mainichi kōen de watashi wa hashirimasu.
examples.en: Every day in the park, I run. (rearranged, verb still last)

rules.title: Dropping subjects and objects
rules.body: Any element that is clear from context is left out, especially I and you: 行きますか — はい、行きます. The listener fills in the gaps from the situation and from politeness forms. Repeating 私 in every sentence sounds self-centred, and あなた is avoided in favour of the person's name.

examples.target: 行きますか。— はい、行きます。
examples.en: Are you going? — Yes, I am.

examples.target: 食べましたか。— いいえ、まだです。
examples.en: Have you eaten? — No, not yet.

examples.target: 田中さんは学生ですか。— はい、そうです。
examples.roman: Tanaka-san wa gakusei desu ka. — Hai, sō desu.
examples.en: Are you a student, Mr Tanaka? — Yes, I am.

rules.title: Question word + か, も, でも
rules.body: Adding か to a question word makes an indefinite: 何か (something), 誰か (someone), どこか (somewhere), いつか (some day). Adding も with a negative gives 'nothing, no one, nowhere': 何も食べませんでした (I ate nothing), 誰もいません. Adding でも gives 'anything, anyone': 何でもいいです (anything is fine).

examples.target: 何も食べませんでした。

exercises.q: Which word refers to a thing near the listener?
exercises.explain: それ is 'that near you'; これ is near the speaker and あれ far from both.

exercises.q: ___は何ですか。(What is this? thing near me)
exercises.explain: これ points to something near the speaker.

exercises.q: あれ refers to something far from both the speaker and the listener.
exercises.explain: The あ series marks distance from both parties.

exercises.answer: これ は 何 です か

exercises.q: この, その and あの are used:
exercises.explain: The -の forms must be followed by a noun: この本.

exercises.q: ___本は私のです。(That book near you is mine.)
exercises.explain: その + noun points to something near the listener.

exercises.q: Japanese is a subject-object-verb language: the verb comes last.
exercises.explain: The predicate always closes the sentence.

exercises.q: How is 何時ですか read?
exercises.explain: 何 is read なん before a counter such as 時.

exercises.answer: トイレ は どこ です か

exercises.q: 誰___来ますか。(Who is coming? subject)
exercises.explain: A question word as subject takes が.

exercises.q: Which sentence has the normal word order?
options: 私は毎日公園で走ります
私は走ります毎日公園で
走ります私は公園で毎日
公園で私は走ります毎日
exercises.explain: Topic, time, place, verb: the verb must come last.

exercises.q: In a Japanese question the question word moves to the front of the sentence.
exercises.explain: The question word stays where the answer would be: 何を飲みますか.

exercises.q: 何___飲みますか。(What will you drink? object)
exercises.explain: 何 replaces the object, so it takes を.

exercises.answer: あなた は いつ 日本 に 来ました か
exercises.en: When did you come to Japan?

exercises.q: What does 何も食べませんでした mean?
exercises.explain: 何も with a negative verb means 'nothing'.

exercises.q: 何___飲みますか。(Will you drink something?)
exercises.explain: 何か means 'something'.

exercises.q: 誰か means 'someone' and 誰も with a negative means 'no one'.
exercises.explain: か makes an indefinite and も + negative a universal negative.

exercises.q: In which phrase is 何 read なに?
exercises.explain: Before particles like を, が and も, 何 is なに; before です and counters it is なん.

exercises.answer: あの 人 は 誰 です か
exercises.en: Who is that person over there?

exercises.q: 日本語の勉強は___ですか。(How is your Japanese study going?)
exercises.explain: どう asks 'how'.

exercises.q: Which reply to 行きますか means 'Yes, I'll go' with the subject dropped?
exercises.explain: The verb alone is a complete answer; the subject is understood.

exercises.q: どちら is a polite way to ask 'which (of two)' or 'where'.
exercises.explain: The こちら series is the polite counterpart of ここ and これ.

exercises.q: ___レストランがいいですか。(What kind of restaurant is good?)
exercises.explain: どんな + noun asks 'what kind of'.

exercises.answer: 田中さん は どこ で 働いて います か

exercises.q: 'Which one is yours?'
options: どれがあなたのですか
どのがあなたのですか
どこがあなたのですか
どうがあなたのですか
exercises.explain: どれ stands alone as a pronoun; どの needs a noun after it.

exercises.q: Time expressions usually come before the place and the object in a Japanese sentence.
exercises.explain: The default order is topic, time, place, object, verb.

sections.title: Counting, time and wanting/liking
sections.summary: This chapter brings together numbers and the sound changes they undergo with counters, telling the time with 時 and 分, and three everyday patterns: wanting to do something (〜たい), liking (〜が好き) and suggesting or inviting (〜ましょう / 〜ませんか).

rules.title: Numbers
rules.body: The Sino-Japanese numbers are 一 ichi, 二 ni, 三 san, 四 yon/shi, 五 go, 六 roku, 七 nana/shichi, 八 hachi, 九 kyū/ku, 十 jū. Tens are 二十 nijū, 三十 sanjū; 百 hyaku (100), 千 sen (1,000), 万 man (10,000). Large numbers group by ten thousand: 一万 is 10,000 and 十万 is 100,000. Some hundreds change sound: 三百 sanbyaku, 六百 roppyaku, 八百 happyaku; 三千 sanzen, 八千 hassen.

rules.title: Numbers with counters and sound changes
rules.body: A counter follows the number, and certain numbers change before counters beginning with h, k, s or t. With 本: 一本 ippon, 三本 sanbon, 六本 roppon, 八本 happon, 十本 juppon. With 分 (minutes): 一分 ippun, 三分 sanpun, 六分 roppun, 十分 juppun. With 冊: 一冊 issatsu, 八冊 hassatsu. 四, 七 and 九 are usually よん, なな, きゅう before counters, but time uses よじ, しちじ, くじ.

examples.target: ビールを一本ください。

rules.title: Telling the hour with 時
rules.body: Hours are number + 時 (ji): 一時 ichiji, 二時 niji, 三時 sanji, 四時 yoji, 五時 goji, 六時 rokuji, 七時 shichiji, 八時 hachiji, 九時 kuji, 十時 jūji, 十一時 jūichiji, 十二時 jūniji. Note the irregular 四時, 七時 and 九時. 午前 (a.m.) and 午後 (p.m.) go before the hour; 半 (half past) goes after: 六時半 (6:30). Ask the time with 今何時ですか.

examples.target: 今何時ですか。— 四時です。
examples.roman: Ima nanji desu ka. — Yoji desu.
examples.en: What time is it? — It's four o'clock.

examples.target: 午後三時に会いましょう。
毎朝六時半に起きます。
examples.en: I get up at half past six every morning.

rules.title: Minutes with 分
rules.body: Minutes are number + 分, read ふん or ぷん depending on the number: 一分 ippun, 二分 nifun, 三分 sanpun, 四分 yonpun, 五分 gofun, 六分 roppun, 七分 nanafun, 八分 happun (or hachifun), 九分 kyūfun, 十分 juppun; 何分 nanpun (how many minutes). Hours come first: 三時五分 (3:05), 十時十五分 (10:15). 前 after a time means 'to': 五時五分前 (five to five).

examples.target: 何分かかりますか。— 十分です。
examples.en: How many minutes does it take? — Ten minutes.

rules.title: Points in time versus durations
rules.body: 二時 (niji) is two o'clock, a point; 二時間 (nijikan) is two hours, a duration. Likewise 五分 is both 'five minutes past' and 'five minutes long', and 一週間 is one week, 三か月 three months, 二年 (間) two years. Points in time take に (三時に会います); durations take no particle (二時間勉強しました).

examples.en: I'll meet you at two o'clock.

examples.target: 二時間日本語を勉強しました。
examples.en: I studied Japanese for two hours.

rules.title: Wanting to do: 〜たい
rules.body: Verb stem (the part before ます) + たい means 'want to': 食べたい (want to eat), 行きたい (want to go), したい (want to do). 〜たい behaves like an i-adjective: 行きたくない (don't want to go), 行きたかった (wanted to go), polite 行きたいです. The object may take が or を: 寿司が食べたい / 寿司を食べたい. 〜たい states the speaker's own wish; for others, use 〜たがっています or report their words.

examples.en: I want to go to Japan.

examples.target: 今日は何もしたくないです。
examples.roman: Kyō wa nani mo shitakunai desu.
examples.en: I don't want to do anything today.

rules.title: Wanting a thing: 〜がほしい
rules.body: To want an object, use noun + がほしい: 新しい車がほしいです (I want a new car). ほしい is an i-adjective: ほしくない, ほしかった. Like 〜たい, it is normally used for the speaker's own wishes or to ask the listener's: 何がほしいですか (What do you want?).

examples.target: 新しい車がほしいです。
今は何もほしくないです。
examples.roman: Ima wa nani mo hoshikunai desu.

rules.title: Liking and being good at: 〜が好き, 上手
rules.body: 好き (like), 嫌い (dislike), 上手 (good at) and 下手 (bad at) are na-adjectives, and the thing liked or the skill takes が: 寿司が好きです, テニスが上手です. 大好き means 'love, like very much'. Being na-adjectives, they negate with じゃありません: 肉はあまり好きじゃありません. Before a noun they take な: 好きな食べ物 (favourite food).

examples.target: 私はテニスが上手じゃありません。
examples.roman: Watashi wa tenisu ga jōzu ja arimasen.

examples.target: 好きな食べ物は何ですか。
examples.roman: Suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka.

rules.title: Suggesting and inviting: 〜ましょう, 〜ましょうか, 〜ませんか
rules.body: Replace ます with ましょう for 'let's': 行きましょう (let's go). 〜ましょうか means 'shall I / shall we?' and is used to offer help or propose: 手伝いましょうか (Shall I help?). 〜ませんか is a polite invitation, 'won't you ... (with me)?': 一緒に映画を見ませんか. Accept with ええ、いいですね or 〜ましょう; decline softly with すみません、ちょっと….

examples.target: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.roman: Issho ni hirugohan o tabemasen ka.
examples.en: Won't you have lunch with me?

examples.target: コーヒーを飲みましょうか。

exercises.q: How is 四時 (four o'clock) read?
exercises.explain: The hours 4, 7 and 9 are irregular: よじ, しちじ, くじ.

exercises.q: 寿司___好きです。(I like sushi; particle)
exercises.explain: The thing liked takes が with 好き.

exercises.q: 九時 is read くじ, not きゅうじ.
exercises.explain: Nine o'clock uses the reading く.

exercises.answer: 一緒 に 映画 を 見ませんか
exercises.en: Won't you watch a film with me?

exercises.q: 'I want to eat sushi':
options: 寿司が食べほしいです
exercises.explain: 〜たい attaches to the verb stem 食べ and takes です for politeness.

exercises.q: 日本に行き___です。(I want to go to Japan.)
exercises.explain: Stem + たい expresses the speaker's wish.

exercises.q: 〜たい conjugates like an i-adjective: 行きたくない, 行きたかった.
exercises.explain: たい ends in い and follows the i-adjective pattern.

exercises.q: How is 七時 (seven o'clock) read?
exercises.explain: Seven o'clock is しちじ in standard Japanese.

exercises.answer: 毎朝 六時 半 に 起きます
exercises.en: I get up at half past six every morning.

exercises.q: 今、三時___です。(It's five past three; ごふん)
exercises.explain: Minutes follow the hour: 三時五分.

exercises.q: What does 〜ましょう mean?
exercises.explain: ます → ましょう makes a proposal including the speaker.

exercises.q: 二時 means 'two hours'.
exercises.explain: 二時 is two o'clock; two hours is 二時間.

exercises.q: 新しい車___ほしいです。(I want a new car.)
exercises.explain: The thing wanted takes が with ほしい.

exercises.answer: コーヒー を 飲みましょう か

exercises.q: How is 三人 read?
exercises.explain: From three on, people are counted with regular number + にん.

exercises.q: 行き___です。(I don't want to go; polite)
exercises.explain: たい negates like an i-adjective: たくない.

exercises.q: 一万 means one thousand.
exercises.explain: 一万 is ten thousand; one thousand is 千.

exercises.q: What does 午後三時 mean?
exercises.explain: 午後 is 'afternoon / p.m.' and goes before the hour.

exercises.answer: 私 は テニス が 上手 じゃ ありません

exercises.q: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べ___か。(Won't you have lunch with me? invitation)
exercises.explain: 〜ませんか is the polite invitation form.

exercises.q: How is 三百 read?
exercises.explain: 百 is voiced to びゃく after 三.

exercises.q: 六百 is read ろっぴゃく.
exercises.explain: 六 becomes ろっ and 百 becomes ぴゃく.

exercises.q: 今、何___ですか。(What time is it now?)
exercises.explain: 何時 (なんじ) asks the hour.

exercises.answer: 二時間 日本語 を 勉強しました
exercises.en: I studied Japanese for two hours.

exercises.q: 水が飲みたい and 水を飲みたい:
exercises.explain: The object of 〜たい may take either が or を.

exercises.q: 〜たい is normally used for the speaker's own wishes, not to describe a third person's.
exercises.explain: For others, Japanese uses 〜たがっています or reports what they said.
